title: Théorie arithmétique. Théorie de Galois des motifs (1965) : notes manuscites (s.d.), tapuscrit (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
This page is not a Grothendieck manuscript page. It is a typed Bourbaki draft, scanned upside down: the header reads '1 - 48 -  n° 413', and Bourbaki numbered its draft rédactions this way. The sheet was evidently reused as scrap paper, and Grothendieck's handwritten notes on motivic Galois groups and anabelian schemes are on the neighbouring pages (presumably the other side of the sheet). The archive numbering '215' is handwritten on it.

The typed content is §17, 'Noyaux de groupe', meaning local Lie groups. Definition 5 says:
- A 'noyau' (germ, or pointed manifold) of class C^r is a C^r manifold V with a marked point e.
- A 'noyau de groupe' is such a germ G with a C^r map θ: G→G (the inverse) and a C^r multiplication m defined on an open set Ω(G) ⊂ G×G.
- These satisfy (i) the inverse axiom (36), (ii) the unit axiom (37), and (iii) associativity (38) wherever both sides are defined.

The text then proves two consequences:
- θ(e)=e, since e = m(e,θ(e)) = θ(e) by (ii).
- θ∘θ = id. Write x = m(e,x) = m(m(θθx,θx),x), apply associativity, then use (i) and (ii) to get θθx.

Example 1: any Lie group is a local Lie group.

Example 2: given a partially defined multiplication satisfying only the unit and associativity axioms, a 'Lemma 1 of n° 3' (implicit-function-type existence of local inverses) gives an open neighbourhood G of e and an involutive diffeomorphism θ satisfying (i). Restricting Ω to pairs whose product stays in G then gives a local group structure. This is the standard notion of local (Lie) group, as in Bourbaki, Groupes et algèbres de Lie, Ch. III, §1 ('groupes de Lie locaux / lois de groupe locales'). It is unrelated to the motivic mathematics on the surrounding pages.
errors: In (iii) the typescript says 'm(x,m(y,z)) appartiennent à Ω'; it should read '(x,m(y,z)) appartiennent à Ω'. This is a typo in the original.
The derivation θθx = x silently uses that (θθx,θx) ∈ Ω and (θθx,e) ∈ Ω. Both follow from (i) and (ii) applied to θx and θθx, so the gap is harmless.
In Example 2 one should also check that Ω(G) is open and contains the required pairs, and that θ preserves G. This is routine but left implicit.

ideas.what: Definition of a local group (noyau de groupe) of class C^r with partially defined multiplication, inverse and the local axioms; proof that the inverse is an involution fixing e
ideas.usually_credited_to: Classical (Lie, Cartan, Pontryagin); systematized by Bourbaki, Groupes et algèbres de Lie Ch. III
ideas.where_published: Bourbaki, Groupes et algèbres de Lie, Ch. III §1 (published version of this draft material)

ideas.what: A local multiplication satisfying unit and associativity admits a local inverse after shrinking (via an implicit-function lemma)
ideas.modern_name: existence of inverses in local groups (implicit function theorem)
ideas.where_published: Bourbaki, Groupes et algèbres de Lie Ch. III

deep.surprise_reason: This is a reused Bourbaki typescript sheet (draft n° 413) on local Lie groups with standard content, not Grothendieck's mathematics. It has no connection to the motivic notes on the adjacent pages.
transcription_corrections: The page image is upside down (rotated 180°). The transcription reads it correctly.
The header '1 - 48 -  n° 413' is a Bourbaki rédaction number, indicating the sheet is a Bourbaki draft reused as scrap paper.
The original (iii) reads 'et m(x,m(y,z)) appartiennent', which is a typo for '(x,m(y,z))'. The transcription reproduces it faithfully.
θ is typed with a stylized theta glyph; Ω is a hand-drawn Omega.
